text.text: Background: Sickle cell anaemia (SCA) is a major public health problem in Uganda.
Monthly sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) remains the standard malaria chemoprevention regimen despite widespread antifolate resistance in East Africa.
We assessed Pfdhfr and Pfdhps resistance mutations and the complexity of infection (COI) among children with SCA receiving malaria chemoprevention.

Methods: This prospective study of antifolate resistance was nested within the CHEMCHA randomised controlled trial comparing monthly SP with weekly dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP) for malaria chemoprevention.
Participants were children with SCA aged 6 months to 15 years and attending Jinja and Kitgum hospitals in Uganda.
Dried blood spots were collected at enrolment, study closeout, and during febrile episodes.
Parasite DNA from microscopyconfirmed clinical malaria samples was genotyped by amplicon sequencing for Pfdhfr (N51I, C59R, S108N, and I164L) and Pfdhps (A437G, K540E, A581G, A613S, and A613T).
COI was estimated using MOIRE.
Results: Complete Pfdhfr/Pfdhps haplotypes were resolved for 7-28 isolates per site and time point, and COI was estimated for 67 samples.
The quintuple mutant (Pfdhfr IRN/Pfdhps GE) accounted for 85.7-100% of isolates across sites and time points; A613S and A613T were not detected.
Pfdhfr I164L was detected in 2/9 isolates in Jinja at baseline and 1/8 at endline.

The Pfdhps A581G mutant allele was absent at baseline (0/44 isolates) but was found in 1/8 isolates in Jinja and 3/34 in Kitgum at endline, including quintuple-plus-581G (sextuple) haplotypes in 1/8 and 2/27 isolates, respectively.
Most infections were monoclonal (51/67, 76.1%).

The high prevalence of quintuple antifolate-resistant haplotypes and the detection of higher-level resistance markers, including emerging sextuple mutants carrying Pfdhfr I164L and Pfdhps A581G, call into question the continued use of SP for chemoprevention in children with SCA in Uganda and support evaluation of alternative regimens.
Sickle cell anaemia (SCA) is a major public health problem, with more than 300,000 affected births annually worldwide, approximately 75% of which occur in sub-Saharan Africa [1].
text.formatted: Sickle cell anaemia (SCA) is a major public health problem, with more than 300,000 affected births annually worldwide, approximately 75% of which occur in sub-Saharan Africa <ref type="bibr">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Global projections suggest that this burden will increase to 400,000 births per year by 2050 [2].
text.formatted: Global projections suggest that this burden will increase to 400,000 births per year by 2050 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[2]</ref>.

text.text: In Uganda, an estimated 15,000-20,000 infants are born with SCA each year [3], and 50%-90% of affected children die before the age of two years [4].
text.formatted: In Uganda, an estimated 15,000-20,000 infants are born with SCA each year <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[3]</ref>, and 50%-90% of affected children die before the age of two years <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Beyond early mortality, children with SCA experience recurrent complications, including painful vaso-occlusive crises, haemolytic episodes, and severe anaemia, many of which are precipitated by febrile illnesses such as malaria [5].
text.formatted: Beyond early mortality, children with SCA experience recurrent complications, including painful vaso-occlusive crises, haemolytic episodes, and severe anaemia, many of which are precipitated by febrile illnesses such as malaria <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Although sickle cell trait (HbAS) confers partial protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria [6], children with SCA remain at substantially increased risk of death from malaria [5].

text.text: Malaria contributes to morbidity in this population by exacerbating chronic anaemia, a determinant of poor clinical outcomes, and precipitating severe SCA complications.

Malaria chemoprevention is therefore a critical component of comprehensive SCA management and has the potential to reduce severe malaria-related morbidity, hospitalisation, blood transfusion requirements, and mortality.
In Uganda, malaria chemoprevention with monthly SP is the standard of care in children with SCA [1].
text.formatted: In Uganda, malaria chemoprevention with monthly SP is the standard of care in children with SCA <ref type="bibr">[1]</ref>.

text.text: However, prolonged SP use across East Africa has been associated with the emergence and selection of drug-resistant P. falciparum [2].
text.formatted: However, prolonged SP use across East Africa has been associated with the emergence and selection of drug-resistant P. falciparum <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Over 90% of P. falciparum isolates in the East African region carry mutations in the dihydrofolate reductase (Pfdhfr) and dihydropteroate synthetase (Pfdhps) genes associated with reduced SP efficacy [3] [4] [5] [6].

text.text: The quintuple mutant haplotype comprising Pfdhfr mutations N51I, C59R, and S108N together with Pfdhps mutations A437G and K540E is an established molecular marker of SP treatment failure [7, 8].

text.text: Some preventive benefit may remain in settings where the prevalence of the Pfdhps K540E mutation is below 50% [9].

text.text: Yet, the continued recommendation of SP for chemoprevention in Ugandan children with SCA, despite well-documented regional resistance, leaves an important gap between policy and the available evidence.
Despite widespread use, few data characterise molecular markers of antimalarial resistance in children with SCA.

It remains unclear whether resistance profiles in this population are comparable to those observed in the general paediatric population, or whether chemoprevention in this group may selectively drive distinct resistance patterns.
These evidence gaps have direct implications for malaria control policy in this high-risk group.
Unlike the general paediatric population, in whom SP exposure is intermittent, children with SCA in Uganda receive monthly SP continuously for years.
Sustained drug pressure may itself select for resistant parasites, and any loss of efficacy carries a disproportionate clinical cost in a group already at high risk of severe malaria.

This study therefore determined the molecular markers of antimalarial resistance in children with SCA receiving malaria chemoprevention in Uganda, to inform malaria prevention strategies and policy in this population.
This was a nested prospective study of antifolate resistance in children with SCA in Uganda.

The study was nested within a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled clinical trial of weekly DP versus monthly SP for malaria chemoprevention in children with SCA (CHEMCHA trial) [10].
text.formatted: The study was nested within a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled clinical trial of weekly DP versus monthly SP for malaria chemoprevention in children with SCA (CHEMCHA trial) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[10]</ref>.

text.text: The parent trial was conducted at two hospitals in Uganda (Jinja Regional Referral Hospital [RRH] and Kitgum General Hospital) and two hospitals in Malawi from April 2021 to May 2023 [10, 11].
text.formatted: The parent trial was conducted at two hospitals in Uganda (Jinja Regional Referral Hospital [RRH] and Kitgum General Hospital) and two hospitals in Malawi from April 2021 to May 2023 <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">11]</ref>.

text.text: This substudy was restricted to the two Ugandan sites, both of which lie in areas with high-grade P. falciparum antifolate resistance.

The sample size for the parent trial was calculated to provide 90% power (two-sided α=0.05) to detect a 50% reduction in the incidence of clinical malaria, from an assumed 0.2 episodes per person-year in the SP arm to 0.1 episodes per person-year in the DP arm [11].

text.text: This required 824 person-years of follow-up in approximately 548 participants [10].

Participants in the main study [10] were 725 children aged 6 months to 15 years with a diagnosis of SCA on haemoglobin electrophoresis or isoelectric focusing.

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to one of two malaria chemoprevention regimens using a computer-generated block randomisation sequence with randomly varying block sizes of 4, 6, or 8, stratified by site and weight category [10].

text.text: Participants attended scheduled clinics with their caregivers every 2 months to receive their next doses of study medication, and unscheduled visits if they were unwell.

At each study visit, participants receiving SP were provided with two additional doses to cover the subsequent two months, while participants receiving DP were provided with doses sufficient to cover 8 weeks; these additional doses were dispensed on the last day of the preceding scheduled visit.
Participants also attended the clinic for all sick visits, including episodes of febrile illnesses.
The study provided standard-of-care clinical services for all unscheduled visits.
Parents or guardians were instructed on home management of children with SCA and on bringing children to the study clinic after identifying signs requiring medical attention [10, 11].

Dried blood Spots (DBS) were packaged according to the principles of triple packaging and transported to the National Malaria Reference and Research Laboratory (NMRRL) using the National Health Laboratory Diagnostics System (NHLDS) hub transportation system [12].

text.text: The primary container was the DBS cards on which blood was spotted.
DBS was wrapped in zip-lock bags (secondary containers) alongside desiccants and sterile cotton gauze.
Together with the filled Laboratory investigation forms and ice packs, the zip-lock bag was put inside a cool box (tertiary container).
The entire package was handed over to the NHLDS hub transport system.
Parasite genomic DNA from all microscopy-positive samples was extracted from blood spots using Tween-20/Chelex 100 as previously described [13].
text.formatted: Parasite genomic DNA from all microscopy-positive samples was extracted from blood spots using Tween-20/Chelex 100 as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, 6-mm diameter discs were punched from dried blood spots into 1.5-mL microcentrifuge tubes and incubated in 0.05% PBS-T [Tween 20 (Sigma Aldrich P9416) in 1× PBS (Corning 21-040-CV)] overnight at 4 °C. Samples then underwent centrifugation at 13,000 rpm for 1 min; the PBS-T was aspirated and replaced with 1 mL of 1× PBS, and the sample was incubated at 4 °C for 30 min.
Following 5 min of centrifugation at 13,000 rpm and 4 °C, the supernatant was aspirated, and 150 µL of 7% Chelex 100 (Bio-Rad 1422822) in water was added.
The sample was then incubated with shaking at 95 °C for 10 min.
Following centrifugation at 13,000 rpm for 10 min, the supernatant containing extracted DNA was transferred to 1.5-mL sample storage tubes, avoiding transfer of any remaining Chelex beads.
Extracted DNA was stored at -20 °C. Parasite density was estimated using quantitative PCR targeting the varATS gene, as previously described [13].

text.text: Samples positive by varATS were selected for genotyping.

Most had low parasitemia.
In Kitgum, a higher proportion, 36/190, tested positive at the start of the study and an even higher proportion (54/190) at study end.

text.text: For Pfdhfr, the N51I and S108N mutants were present in all isolates and at both sites and time points (N51I: 11/11 and 8/8 in Jinja, and 31/31 and 32/32 in Kitgum, at the start of the study and at endline, respectively; S108N: 9/9 and 8/8 in Jinja, and 30/30 and 31/31 in Kitgum).

C59R was mutant in all isolates at the start of the study (11/11 in Jinja and 31/31 in Kitgum) and in all isolates in Jinja at endline (8/8); in Kitgum at endline it was mutant in 29/32 isolates, and 3/32 were wild type.
The I164L mutation was detected in 2/9 isolates in Jinja at the start of the study and in 1/8 at endline.
In Kitgum, it was not detected at the start of the study (0/30), and one isolate at endline had a mixed genotype (1/31).

For Pfdhps, the K540E mutation was detected in 7/8 isolates in Jinja and 28/30 in Kitgum at the start of the study (with two mixed genotypes in Kitgum), and in 8/8 and 31/33 isolates at endline, respectively.

The A437G mutation was detected in 1/8 isolates in Jinja and 1/30 in Kitgum at the start of the study (with one further mixed genotype in Kitgum), and in 0/8 and 1/36 isolates at endline, respectively.
The A581G mutation was not detected at the start of the study although one isolate in Kitgum had a mixed genotype (1/34).
At endline, the A581G mutant allele was detected in 1/8 isolates in Jinja and 3/34 isolates in Kitgum.
A613S and A613T were wild type in all isolates at both sites and time points (Jinja: 10/10 at the start of the study and 8/8 at endline; Kitgum: 30/30 at both time points).
The quintuple mutant haplotype (IRN plus GE) predominated at both sites and at both time points (Fig. 4A).

text.text: In Jinja, it was detected in 6/7 isolates at the start of the study and in 8/8 at endline, and in Kitgum in 25/26 and 24/28, respectively.
Other haplotypes were uncommon.
They were IRN plus AK in Jinja at the start of the study (1/7,), and ICN plus GE (2/28,), IRN plus AK (1/28), and IRN plus GK (1/28) in Kitgum at endline.
The quintuple plus 581G haplotype, which corresponds to the sextuple mutant, was not detected in Jinja at the start of the study (0/7) but was detected in 1/8 isolates at endline.
In Kitgum, it was detected in 1/26 isolates at the start of the study and in 2/27 at endline (Fig. 4B).

Most infections were monoclonal (51/67, 76.1%), followed by infections with a COI of 2 (12/67, 17.9%).
COI values of 3 and 4 were each observed in 2/67 samples (3.0%) (Fig. 3).

text.text: This study characterised molecular markers of antifolate resistance and the COI among Plasmodium falciparum parasites infecting children with SCA receiving malaria chemoprevention in Jinja and Kitgum, Uganda, at enrolment and at the end of follow-up.
The Pfdhfr N51I, C59R, S108N, and Pfdhps K540E and A437G mutations were present in nearly all successfully genotyped isolates.
At the haplotype level, the Pfdhfr IRN/Pfdhps GE quintuple-mutant background predominated at both sites and time points.
Additional markers associated with higherlevel antifolate resistance, Pfdhfr I164L and Pfdhps A581G, were also detected.

These findings are particularly relevant in the context of the parent CHEMCHA trial, in which the incidence of clinical malaria was approximately five times higher among children receiving monthly SP than among those receiving weekly DP [10].
text.formatted: These findings are particularly relevant in the context of the parent CHEMCHA trial, in which the incidence of clinical malaria was approximately five times higher among children receiving monthly SP than among those receiving weekly DP <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[10]</ref>.

text.text: The appearance of A581G during follow-up, in parasites causing breakthrough malaria in children taking monthly SP, is consistent with selection of the most resistant parasites under continuous drug pressure.

These data argue for revision of the Ugandan recommendation of monthly SP for children with sickle cell anaemia: weekly DP is the evidence-based alternative in children younger than 5 years receiving penicillin prophylaxis [10]; further evaluation is needed in older children, and continuing SP in this group risks selecting for parasites carrying still higher-level antifolate resistance.

text.text: At baseline, a higher proportion of the samples from Kitgum had parasite densities exceeding 1000 parasites/µL, consistent with the higher transmission intensity of that region [15].

text.text: At endline, parasite densities in Kitgum shifted toward lower strata, which may indicate partial suppression of high-density infections by chemoprevention.
However, the persistence of infections in the 1-10 and 101-1000 parasites/µL strata also suggests ongoing low-grade transmission despite prophylaxis.
In Jinja, parasite density distributions were broadly stable at the beginning of the study and endline, consistent with its peri-urban setting.

The prevalence and pattern of Pfdhfr and Pfdhps mutations observed in this study, including the near-universal quintuple mutant haplotype, are similar to those reported in general paediatric and antenatal populations elsewhere in East Africa [5].

text.text: This suggests that children with SCA are not exposed to a distinct resistance profile compared with the wider population, although their continuous use of SP chemoprevention may increase the clinical consequences of existing resistance.

The high prevalence of the Pfdhfr N51I, C59R, and S108N mutations, which together constitute the triple mutant (IRN) haplotype conferring high-level pyrimethamine resistance, at both study sites is also consistent with previous evidence showing that these variants are already highly prevalent across East Africa [2, 3, 5].

text.text: Their presence at or close to 100% at both time points and at both sites suggests that these mutations are now fixed, or nearly fixed, in the local parasite population.
Similarly, the high prevalence of the Pfdhps A437G (88-100%) and K540E (88-95%) mutations indicates that the quintuple mutant haplotype is dominant in this population.
Haplotype-level analysis confirmed this pattern.

The full quintuple mutant (Pfdhfr IRN/Pfdhps GE) accounted for 86-100% of isolates in Jinja and 86-96% of isolates in Kitgum at baseline and endline, with only a small proportion of isolates carrying partial mutant backgrounds.

The presence of the quintuple mutant among children with SCA is particularly concerning because these children receive monthly SP chemoprevention continuously over several years, unlike the general paediatric population, in whom SP exposure is typically intermittent.
Sustained drug pressure in this population may reduce the protective benefit of SP and favour the persistence or further selection of resistant parasite populations.
The presence of both I164L and A581G in this population deserves attention because these mutations have been uncommon in Uganda [6] and mediate high-level SP resistance [16].

text.text: In a 2024 survey of children with malaria in northern, north-eastern and eastern Uganda, I164L was found in a few samples, and A581G was reported as a mixed genotype [17].

text.text: By contrast, the Pfdhps A581G mutant allele, which was not detected at baseline, was found at endline at both sites.

One possible explanation is selection by continued SP exposure, since SP given for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy in Uganda has been associated with selection of I164L and A581G [5, 18].

text.text: The presence of the quintuple and sextuple haplotype is particularly relevant in children with SCA, who receive monthly SP chemoprevention continuously over several years, in contrast to the more intermittent SP exposure typically experienced by the general paediatric population.

Given that a Pfdhps K540E prevalence above 50% has been associated with reduced preventive efficacy of SP [9], the levels observed here (88-95%) suggest that SP chemoprevention may already provide suboptimal protection for children with SCA in Uganda, and there is a need to revise the malaria chemoprevention policies.

text.text: The predominance of monoclonal infections across both sites may reflect suppression of polyclonal parasite populations by continuous chemoprevention.

Previous studies in Uganda have reported polyclonal infections in more than 50% of samples across sites of varying transmission intensity, in community-based cohorts of children (6 months-10 years) [19].

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that most circulating parasites in this population carry a molecular profile associated with SP treatment failure.
This raises important concerns about the continued use of SP as the standard chemoprevention regimen for children with SCA in Uganda and supports re-evaluation of the current malaria policy.
This study has several limitations.

It was a secondary analysis nested within a clinical trial, and the sample sizes at individual sites and time points were relatively small, which may have limited the precision of the haplotype-frequency estimates.

The analysis was also restricted to the Ugandan trial sites; therefore, the findings may not be generalisable to settings with different transmission intensities, resistance profiles, or chemoprevention histories.
In addition, the data are not linked to individual clinical outcomes; therefore, no inferences can be drawn about the association between a specific haplotype and the risk of clinical malaria.
Molecular markers of SP resistance are near universal among children with SCA receiving malaria chemoprevention in Uganda.

The quintuple mutant haplotype predominated at both sites, Pfdhfr I164L was present from baseline, and Pfdhps A581G, undetected at baseline, appeared at endline in parasites causing breakthrough malaria, consistent with selection of sextuple mutants under continuous monthly SP.
The profile is no different from that of the wider parasite population, but its consequences are, because these children take SP every month for years and are at high risk of severe malaria.
Taken with the five-fold higher incidence of clinical malaria in the SP arm of the parent trial, these findings indicate that monthly SP is no longer adequate chemoprevention in this group.

Weekly DP should replace it in children younger than 5 years receiving penicillin prophylaxis; its efficacy and safety should be established in older children, and molecular surveillance should continue under whichever regimen is adopted.
